subject: Cloud Computing
title: Cloud Databases
description: A micro-lesson that makes Cloud Databases usable.

hook.text: Every app needs a database. In the cloud, you can launch one in minutes without managing a server.

buildup.text: Managed databases handle backups, patches, and scaling for you. AWS RDS, Azure SQL, Cloud SQL.

discovery.text: You choose the engine — PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB — and the cloud handles the infrastructure.

twist.text: Managed databases cost more than self-hosted ones. You're paying for the labor you don't do.

climax.text: For most teams, the convenience far outweighs the premium. Managing databases is painful work.

punchline.text: Cloud databases: your data, someone else's headache.

quiz.question: What does a 'managed database' service provide?
options: The cloud provider handles backups, patching, and scaling automatically
A database that manages itself with no human input ever needed
Free unlimited storage for any type of data

details.summary: Cloud databases are managed services that handle provisioning, patching, backups, and scaling automatically. From relational databases like RDS and Cloud SQL to NoSQL options like DynamoDB and Firestore, cloud providers offer specialized databases for every data model and access pattern.
details.whyItMatters: Managed databases eliminate the significant operational burden of running databases yourself. Choosing the right database type for your data model is one of the most impactful architecture decisions.
takeaways: Managed databases handle patching, backups, and scaling
Relational, document, key-value, and graph options are available
Serverless database options scale to zero when not in use

faq.question: Should you use a managed or self-managed database?
faq.answer: Managed databases cost more per unit but eliminate the operational cost of patching, monitoring, backup, and failover management. For most organizations, managed databases are more cost-effective when total cost of ownership including personnel time is considered.

faq.question: How do you choose between relational and NoSQL?
faq.answer: Use relational databases for complex queries, transactions, and structured data with relationships. Use NoSQL for high-throughput simple queries, flexible schemas, and horizontal scaling. Many applications use both, choosing the best database for each specific data access pattern.
